highlightAliases.old: CSA is two to three times more prevalent at age 65–90 vs 39–64; upwards of 50% of stable heart-failure patients have some form of SDB (p646).
highlightAliases.new: CSA is two to three times more prevalent at age 65–90 vs 39–64; an estimated upwards of 50% of stable heart-failure patients have some form of SDB (p646).

highlightAliases.old: CPAP pressure usually 5 to 20 cm H2O; well tolerated above age 80 and in mild-moderate dementia (p649).
highlightAliases.new: CPAP pressure usually 5 to 20 cm H2O; observational studies found it well tolerated above age 80 and in mild-moderate dementia (p649).

highlightAliases.old: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation trials limited to BMI less than 32 kg/m2; cohort of 62 patients aged 65–80 showed benefit (p650).
highlightAliases.new: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation trials limited to highly selected CPAP-intolerant patients with BMI less than 32 kg/m2; cohort of 62 patients aged 65–80 showed benefit (p650).

highlightAliases.old: Start iron if ferritin less than 75 mcg/L; consider IV iron if ferritin less than 300 mcg/L with moderate-severe symptoms (p652).
highlightAliases.new: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in clinically significant RLS. AASM guidance considers iron at ferritin ≤75 µg/L or transferrin saturation <20%, with IV iron when ferritin is 75–100 µg/L if iron is indicated. The moderate–severe RLS trial permitting ferritin 75–300 µg/L required transferrin saturation <20% in that range (p652; trial, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

highlightAliases.old: A third of older patients had persistent severe insomnia at 4-year follow-up; more than 80% of women over 85 report sleeping difficulties (p658).
highlightAliases.new: In one study, a third of older patients had persistent severe insomnia at 4-year follow-up; more than 80% of women over 85 report sleeping difficulties (p658).

highlightAliases.old: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects, less amnestic (p660). Suvorexant/lemborexant (DORA) — only suvorexant FDA-approved for insomnia with Alzheimer dementia (trial of 277 patients, mild-moderate AD, sleep time up around half an hour after 2 weeks) (p660). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).
highlightAliases.new: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists for insomnia. The suvorexant trial in mild–moderate probable Alzheimer dementia randomized 285, of whom 277 completed. Placebo-adjusted total sleep time improved by 28 minutes at week 4 (p660; Herring et al., FDA Belsomra prescribing information). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).

highlightAliases.old: Drugs (Table 44-2, p653): Ropinirole 0.25–4 mg, Pramipexole 0.125–2 mg — caution: augmentation, behavioral disinhibition. Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg — reserve for infrequent dosing (highest augmentation risk). Gabapentin enacarbil 600–1200 mg (only α2δ ligand FDA-approved for RLS), gabapentin 100–1800 mg, pregabalin 300 mg — caution: sedation, suicidal ideation. Clonazepam 0.25–2 mg, temazepam 15–30 mg — limited evidence, cognitive risk. Opiate agents (all off-label) for refractory RLS: codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg, methadone 5–10 mg.Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026.
highlightAliases.new: RLS drug selection. The AASM favors gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin when appropriate. FDA-labeled gabapentin enacarbil is 600 mg daily for RLS with normal renal function; 1,200 mg adds adverse effects without additional benefit. Dopamine agonists can cause augmentation and behavioral disinhibition. If pramipexole is chosen, the labeled RLS titration is 0.125–0.5 mg once daily. The labeled ropinirole range begins at 0.25 mg, up to 4 mg daily. Table 44-2 lists carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg for infrequent use because of augmentation. Table 44-2 lists off-label gabapentin 100–1,800 mg and pregabalin 300 mg as studied doses. Adjust for renal function and monitor sedation. The table lists clonazepam 0.25–2 mg and temazepam 15–30 mg, with limited evidence and cognitive/fall risks. Its off-label opioid examples are codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg and methadone 5–10 mg. These are historical table ranges. Specialist assessment of respiratory, dependence and medication risks is essential in refractory RLS (p653; FDA prescribing information for Horizant and pramipexole, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026; Current practice (not the book): AASM conditionally suggests against standard pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine or ropinirole use in adults with RLS because of augmentation with longer-term treatment; evidence certainty is moderate for pramipexole/ropinirole and low for rotigotine; patients prioritizing short-term symptom relief over long-term adverse effects may still choose these agents - AASM 2025, recommendations 12-14, p144

highlightAliases.old: Diagnostic: AHI > 15 alone, or > 5 with symptoms/comorbidities; AHI > 30 = severe (p645).
highlightAliases.new: Adult obstructive sleep apnea can be diagnosed with ≥15 obstructive respiratory events/hour, or ≥5/hour with relevant symptoms or comorbidities. Severe OSA begins at AHI ≥30/hour (p645; ICSD-3-TR, VA/DoD 2025 guideline, Appendix F).

highlightAliases.old: ASV generally not recommended if EF less than 45% (SERVE-HF: increased mortality) (p649).
highlightAliases.new: SERVE-HF found increased mortality with its ASV device in symptomatic chronic heart failure, LVEF ≤45% and predominantly central sleep apnea. Any consideration of ASV in HFrEF requires an experienced center, shared decision-making and close follow-up (p649; SERVE-HF, AASM 2025 central sleep apnea guideline).

highlightAliases.old: PLMS last 0.5 seconds to 10 seconds, 5 to 90 seconds apart; at least four in a row required; PLMD needs at least 15 PLMS/hour (p651).
highlightAliases.new: PLMS last 0.5–10 seconds, occur 5–90 seconds apart and comprise at least four consecutive movements. Adult PLMD requires more than 15 movements/hour with clinically significant sleep disturbance or daytime dysfunction unexplained by another disorder (p651; AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

highlightAliases.old: Start iron if ferritin less than 75 mcg/L; consider IV iron if ferritin less than 300 mcg/L with moderate-severe symptoms, although IV iron is usually reserved for iron malabsorption (p652).
highlightAliases.new: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in clinically significant RLS. AASM guidance considers iron at ferritin ≤75 µg/L or transferrin saturation <20%, with IV iron when ferritin is 75–100 µg/L if iron is indicated. The moderate–severe RLS trial permitting ferritin 75–300 µg/L required transferrin saturation <20% in that range (p652; trial, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).

highlightAliases.old: Chronic if symptoms persist more than 3 months; short-term if fewer than 3 months (p657).
highlightAliases.new: Chronic insomnia causes sleep difficulty despite adequate opportunity, with daytime consequences, at least 3 nights/week for at least 3 months. Short-term insomnia lasts less than 3 months (p657; ICSD-3-TR, VA/DoD 2025 guideline, Appendix F).

Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).

highlightAliases.new: At least 15 obstructive respiratory events/hour suffice, or at least 5/hour with relevant symptoms or comorbidities. An AHI of 30/hour or more is severe (p645; ICSD-3-TR).

highlightAliases.new: In selected longitudinal cohorts, up to 90% of people presenting with isolated RBD developed a clinically evident synucleinopathy (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia, MSA) over 10- to 15-year follow-up (p654).
